html:
Flux through a closed cube
Click a cube face to see its outward normal n and signed flux Φ = E·n·A.
Net flux Φnet
Top FGHK: +EA²
Bottom ABCD: −EA²
4 side faces: 0
Φnet = +EA² − EA² + 0 = 0
No charge enclosed → net flux is zero.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 23: Gauss's Law
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram of a cube sitting in the uniform field between two oppositely charged plates. Two large grey parallelograms are drawn in perspective, one above and one below, labeled '-q' at the right edge of the upper plate and '+q' at the right edge of the lower one; both are covered with short red arrows that all point straight up, and the field itself is named with a vector E at the far left. Between the plates stands a cube with every vertex lettered, A, B, C and D around the bottom face and F, G, H and K around the top, so the bottom face reads ABCD and the top face FGHK. A shaded diagonal plane is drawn inside the cube, running from the upper edge KF down to the lower edge BC and dividing the cube into two wedges. Red field arrows continue through the cube's interior, entering the bottom face and leaving the top face, while the four vertical side faces lie parallel to them. Because the identical arrows enter below and exit above, the reader is meant to tally signed contributions face by face and see them cancel. The arrangement is used to evaluate the flux through a closed surface that encloses no charge.

elements: upper grey plate drawn as a large horizontal parallelogram above the cube, labeled '-q' near its right edge
lower grey plate drawn as a large horizontal parallelogram below the cube, labeled '+q' near its right edge
short red upward field arrows covering both plates (dense scatter, all vertical)
vector E label at the far left of the upper plate
transparent cube centered between the plates with visible edges
bottom cube face ABCD (vertices A, B, C, D)
top cube face FGHK (vertices F, G, H, K)
four vertical side faces of the cube
shaded semi-transparent diagonal plane inside the cube running from top edge KF down to bottom edge BC
red field arrows passing through the cube interior, entering bottom face ABCD and leaving top face FGHK
vertex letter labels A, B, C, D, F, G, H, K at the cube corners

interactions.teaches: Selecting a face shows its outward normal n and the sign of E·n: negative (blue/red coded) for the bottom face where field enters, positive for the top face where it leaves, and zero for the four side faces parallel to E — flux is a signed, face-by-face sum

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching to the net view combines the individual top (+EA²) and bottom (−EA²) contributions into a single sum of zero, showing that equal field entering and leaving means the cube encloses no charge

demo_steps.title: Inspect one face
demo_steps.narration: The learner clicks a face: bottom ABCD shows negative flux (field enters), top FGHK shows positive flux (field leaves), any side face shows zero since E is parallel to it.

demo_steps.title: Sum all faces
demo_steps.narration: Switching to Net flux stacks the six signed contributions: +EA² from the top and −EA² from the bottom cancel, and the four side faces contribute nothing — total flux through the closed cube is zero.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Plates: two identical grey (#9a9a9a, ~0.85 opacity) horizontal PlaneGeometry/parallelograms ~10 × 7 world units, upper at y=+3.4, lower at y=−3.4, drawn with slight perspective tilt so far edges recede toward upper right; '-q' label at right edge of upper plate, '+q' at right edge of lower plate. Cube: side length ~2 units, centered at origin, faces axis-aligned (vertical faces parallel to field). Bottom face ABCD: A front-left, B front-right, C back-right, D back-left; top face FGHK: F above A, G above B... actually per source F sits above A's region left-front, K above-back-left, H above-back-right, G above front-right — keep labels: top face corners F (front-left), G (front-right), H (back-right), K (back-left); bottom A (front-left), B (front-right), C (back-right), D (back-left). Diagonal shaded plane inside cube from top edge KF (left top edge) slanting down to bottom edge BC (right bottom edge), light grey ~0.35 opacity, divides cube into two wedges. Field arrows: red #cc2222 cones/shafts ~0.5 units long, all pointing +Y (straight up); ~25 scattered on each plate plus 4–6 passing vertically through the cube interior (entering through ABCD, exiting through FGHK). Cube edges thin dark grey lines; faces nearly transparent (opacity ~0.06) so interior arrows show. Selected face highlight: green #22aa44 for positive flux, blue #2255cc for negative, neutral grey for zero, with an outward normal arrow (n) drawn from the face center. Colors dominated by grey plates, red arrows, white background.
interactionPlan.notes: Render cube faces as individual meshes so each is independently raycast-clickable and highlightable. On face click, display an annotation sprite near the face with its name, normal direction, and signed Φ = E·n·A value (use symbolic ±EA² / 0). In Net flux view show a stacked bar or equation-style sum of the six contributions animating to 0, with top/bottom faces simultaneously highlighted green/blue. Keep orbit available implicitly via the click-scene, but the two requested interactions carry the lesson; normal arrows should point outward and flip color with sign.

authoredContext:
The figure shows the electric field of an oppositely charged, parallel-plate system and an imaginary box between the plates. The electric field between the plates is uniform and points from the positive plate toward the negative plate. A calculation of the flux of this field through various faces of the box shows that the net flux through the box is zero. Why does the flux cancel out here?

Electric flux through a cube, placed between two charged plates. Electric flux through the bottom face (ABCD) is negative, because E→ is in the opposite direction to the normal to the surface. The electric flux through the top face (FGHK) is positive, because the electric field and the normal are in the same direction. The electric flux through the other faces is zero, since the electric field is perpendicular to the normal vectors of those faces. The net electric flux through the cube is the sum of fluxes through the six faces. Here, the net flux through the cube is equal to zero. The magnitude of the flux through rectangle BCKF is equal to the magnitudes of the flux through both the top and bottom faces.

A cube ABCDKFGH is shown in the center. A diagonal plane is shown within it from KF to BC. The top surface of the cube, FGHK has a plane labeled minus q slightly above it and parallel to it. Similarly, another plane is labeled plus q is shown slightly below the bottom surface of the cube, parallel to it. Small red arrows are shown pointing upwards from the bottom plane, pointing up to the bottom surface of the cube, pointing up from the top surface of the cube and pointing up to the top plane. These are labeled vector E.

The reason is that the sources of the electric field are outside the box. Therefore, if any electric field line enters the volume of the box, it must also exit somewhere on the surface because there is no charge inside for the lines to land on. Therefore, quite generally, electric flux through a closed surface is zero if there are no sources of electric field, whether positive or negative charges, inside the enclosed volume. In general, when field lines leave (or “flow out of”) a closed surface, Φ is positive; when they enter (or “flow into”) the surface, Φ is negative.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Plates: two identical grey (#9a9a9a, ~0.85 opacity) horizontal PlaneGeometry/parallelograms ~10 × 7 world units, upper at y=+3.4, lower at y=−3.4, drawn with slight perspective tilt so far edges recede toward upper right; '-q' label at right edge of upper plate, '+q' at right edge of lower plate. Cube: side length ~2 units, centered at origin, faces axis-aligned (vertical faces parallel to field). Bottom face ABCD: A front-left, B front-right, C back-right, D back-left; top face FGHK: F above A, G above B... actually per source F sits above A's region left-front, K above-back-left, H above-back-right, G above front-right — keep labels: top face corners F (front-left), G (front-right), H (back-right), K (back-left); bottom A (front-left), B (front-right), C (back-right), D (back-left). Diagonal shaded plane inside cube from top edge KF (left top edge) slanting down to bottom edge BC (right bottom edge), light grey ~0.35 opacity, divides cube into two wedges. Field arrows: red #cc2222 cones/shafts ~0.5 units long, all pointing +Y (straight up); ~25 scattered on each plate plus 4–6 passing vertically through the cube interior (entering through ABCD, exiting through FGHK). Cube edges thin dark grey lines; faces nearly transparent (opacity ~0.06) so interior arrows show. Selected face highlight: green #22aa44 for positive flux, blue #2255cc for negative, neutral grey for zero, with an outward normal arrow (n) drawn from the face center. Colors dominated by grey plates, red arrows, white background.
interactionPlan.notes: Render cube faces as individual meshes so each is independently raycast-clickable and highlightable. On face click, display an annotation sprite near the face with its name, normal direction, and signed Φ = E·n·A value (use symbolic ±EA² / 0). In Net flux view show a stacked bar or equation-style sum of the six contributions animating to 0, with top/bottom faces simultaneously highlighted green/blue. Keep orbit available implicitly via the click-scene, but the two requested interactions carry the lesson; normal arrows should point outward and flip color with sign.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram of a cube sitting in the uniform field between two oppositely charged plates. Two large grey parallelograms are drawn in perspective, one above and one below, labeled '-q' at the right edge of the upper plate and '+q' at the right edge of the lower one; both are covered with short red arrows that all point straight up, and the field itself is named with a vector E at the far left. Between the plates stands a cube with every vertex lettered, A, B, C and D around the bottom face and F, G, H and K around the top, so the bottom face reads ABCD and the top face FGHK. A shaded diagonal plane is drawn inside the cube, running from the upper edge KF down to the lower edge BC and dividing the cube into two wedges. Red field arrows continue through the cube's interior, entering the bottom face and leaving the top face, while the four vertical side faces lie parallel to them. Because the identical arrows enter below and exit above, the reader is meant to tally signed contributions face by face and see them cancel. The arrangement is used to evaluate the flux through a closed surface that encloses no charge.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting a cube face: the learner clicks ABCD, FGHK, or a side face, the chosen face normal and E dot n contribution appear with positive, negative, or zero color coding, making signed electric flux a face-by-face sum.
- Toggle between face-sum and net-flux views: the learner switches views, the individual top and bottom contributions are shown separately and then combined to zero, clarifying why equal field entering and leaving means no enclosed charge.

discrepancies: Field arrows are filled uniformly and densely across the entire gap (including through the cube), whereas the source has a sparser, scattered distribution concentrated on the plates and a handful in the gap
The diagonal shaded plane in the source has a distinctly bluish/silver glossy tint, but the generated version renders it as a neutral grey gradient
The source's E label carries a proper vector-arrow glyph; the generated labeling relies on a combining arrow character that may not render consistently
evaluation.notes: Highly faithful reconstruction of the capacitor-plates/cube/flux figure with correct primitives, correct labels, and meaningful, pedagogically-correct face-inspection and net-flux interactions; only minor stylistic deviations in arrow distribution and diagonal-plane tint.
action_items: Reduce the uniform volume arrow density and use jittered scatter tuning so the field looks like the sparser scatter of the source rather than a solid arrow forest
